Recycling igloos labelled PLASTY, PAPÍR, SKLO směs, KOVOVÉ odpady, 'DĚKUJEME VÁM, ŽE TŘÍDÍTE' — Czech (not Slovak, which would use 'sklo zmes / ďakujeme, že triedite').
Yellow/blue/green/grey dome-shaped EKO-KOM style separation containers, the standard Czech municipal waste set (yellow=plastics, blue=paper).
Phone number '723 066 930' — 9-digit Czech mobile format beginning with 7, and an e-mail with .cz TLD.
Older Škoda Fabia/Octavia with the winged-arrow badge dominating traffic, plus VW T4 utility van — typical Czech village fleet.
Diamond-on-pole priority road sign and small white street-name plate on the corner house, standard Czech/Central European practice.

Large hipped-roof former manor/agricultural cooperative building with red clay tiles, painted cream render, adjoining barns with fibre-cement roofing — classic Bohemian village core built around a farmstead complex.
Renovated village houses with steep gables, sgraffito-style render decoration and heavy solar thermal/PV retrofits on the south slopes; wooden picket and concrete-panel fences.

Broad rolling arable plateau at maybe 400-500 m with cereal strips, spruce/deciduous windbreaks and no mountains on the horizon — inner Bohemian upland (Central Bohemian/Tábor-type highland) rather than Alpine foreland or Moravian lowland.
Horse chestnuts in full bloom and lilac flowering, plus clipped box/ligustrum spheres in front gardens — late-May Central European village.

White globe/cone street lanterns on slim galvanised poles, small concrete sculpture on the green, brick-paved sidewalks with red edge strip — post-2010 EU-funded village-centre renewal typical of Czech obce.

Village football pitch with two small covered dugouts and a raised timber commentary/referee box, fenced with panel mesh — standard Czech lower-league village ground, suggesting a village of a few hundred to ~1000 inhabitants.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A well-kept, moderately prosperous Czech farming village: renovated single-family houses with solar panels, tidy clipped hedges, brick-paved footways and new lighting (EU/municipal grant era), a converted agricultural-cooperative building now housing a small firm, and local trades (joinery workshop advertising windows, doors, roofs, fences) serving the surrounding countryside. Car fleet is mid-age Czech/German mass-market, no visible poverty or luxury. Economy = mixed arable farming plus commuting to a nearby district town, with small artisan businesses.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A prosperous, EU-integrated Czech village: rendered family houses in fresh pastel colours, rooftop photovoltaic and solar-thermal installations, tidy brick-paver footways, municipal EKO-KOM sorted-waste igloos and a fenced club football pitch. Employment mixes local micro-enterprise (a joinery workshop advertising bespoke windows, doors, roof trusses and fences) with commuting to a nearby district town; a large courtyard complex from the collectivised era survives as premises for a successor firm, while the surrounding consolidated cereal blocks are still worked at cooperative scale. Overall a middle-income, car-dependent rural commuter belt rather than a subsistence or depopulated periphery.

correction.summary: Full hit: Czechia / South Bohemian Region (Tábor District) / Želeč, 5.3 km error. The Czech-only orthography on the EKO-KOM igloo labels ('PAPÍR', 'SKLO směs', 'DĚKUJEME VÁM, ŽE TŘÍDÍTE') plus the joinery van's 'TRUHLÁŘSTVÍ PÍCHA ŽELEČ' with a .cz address pinned both country and settlement, and the rolling cereal plateau with conifer woodlots (no vineyards) correctly excluded Moravia. Slovakia and Austria were rightly excluded by the absence of ľ/ô/ä spellings and of any German-language waste labels ('ALTPAPIER/ALTGLAS').

discriminators.title: Czech vs Slovak sorted-waste igloo lettering
discriminators.body: On Czech recycling igloos you read 'PAPÍR', 'SKLO', 'PLASTY', 'KOVOVÉ odpady' and 'DĚKUJEME VÁM, ŽE TŘÍDÍTE' with ě and ř. In Slovakia you would instead see 'PAPIER', 'SKLO', 'PLASTY' with ľ/ô/ä forms elsewhere on municipal signage and .sk contacts. The ě/ř pair is the single fastest CZ/SK split at village scale.

discriminators.title: Czech village waste bins vs Austrian German-labelled containers
discriminators.body: Czech villages place clustered fibreglass dome igloos with Czech stream names and EKO-KOM stickers behind a mesh fence. In Austria you would instead find rectangular wheeled or sunken containers labelled 'ALTPAPIER', 'ALTGLAS bunt/weiss' with the ARA logo, and village entry signs in the white-on-blue Austrian format. Absence of any German text rules Austria out even where the house typology looks identical.

discriminators.title: South Bohemian plateau vs Moravian vineyard lowland
discriminators.body: Around Tábor the horizon is an undulating 400-500 m plateau of large cereal blocks with dark spruce woodlots and hedgerows, and village cores show reused courtyard cooperative buildings. In south Moravia you would instead see vineyard rows on slopes, rows of wine cellars along a lane, and often flatter black-soil arable. No vines anywhere is a strong Bohemia signal.

discriminators.title: Tradesman van toponym as district anchor in Czechia
discriminators.body: In Czech villages small joinery/roofing firms paint their base village name plus a .cz mail address on the van, and such vans usually park at their own yard. Use that name to pick the district rather than the country; where a name is duplicated (e.g. a Bohemian and a Moravian homonym), decide with the terrain — rolling plateau with conifer woodlots for Bohemia instead of a dead-flat black-soil plain for Haná.
